Yes. From the provided ATAC-seq peak calls, AI-10-49 treatment is associated with a global change in chromatin accessibility, mainly a reduction in the number and breadth of called accessible regions.

DMSO ATAC-seq replicates had 67,066 and 64,929 MACS2 peaks (mean 65997.5), whereas AI-10-49 replicates had 48,706 and 53,141 peaks (mean 50923.5), a 22.8% decrease after treatment. Total peak-covered genomic span also decreased by 13.0%.

In a merged consensus universe of 103,177 intervals, DMSO-only intervals (39,179) substantially outnumbered AI-10-49-only intervals (13,263). With the stricter criterion of presence in both replicates of one condition and absence in both replicates of the other, 4,801 peaks were lost after AI-10-49 versus 2,007 gained. Mean signal summed over the consensus universe was nearly unchanged, so the strongest supported conclusion is not a uniform genome-wide collapse of ATAC signal, but a global remodeling/reduction in the set of accessible sites.

Thus, AI-10-49 treatment does lead to global chromatin-accessibility changes in inv(16) AML cells, with a net loss of called accessible regions after treatment. This conclusion is descriptive because only peak-call files, not raw BAM/count matrices, were available for formal replicate-aware differential accessibility testing.
